any more. Your mind will be punched in a card

and shut away in a little drawer.

they will call you. When they want you

to die for profit they will let you know.

understand. Praise ignorance, for what man

has not encountered he has not destroyed.

Announcement this week that Lilly will file a BLA for retatrutide has caused a bit of confusion.  Here's what I understand to be the situation:
• Lilly asked FDA to classify retatrutide as a biologic.
• FDA declined, determining that retatrutide should be regulated as a drug under FD&C Act rather than as a biologic under the Public Health Service Act. 
• Lilly challenged that decision in federal court. 
• Lilly lost in the district court.
• In late 2025, the district court upheld FDA's interpretation that retatrutide is not a biologic under the governing statute and regulations. 
• Lilly appealed, arguing that FDA's interpretation is incorrect. That appeal has not yet been finally resolved by the court.

So why are reports now saying Lilly intends to submit a Biologics License Application? Because an applicant can submit whatever application it believes is legally appropriate. Announcing an intent to file a BLA is not the same thing as FDA agreeing that a BLA is the correct regulatory pathway.

The report in Reuters merely says Lilly plans to seek FDA approval in early 2027; it does not say FDA has changed its position on the biologic classification. This distinction matters. If Lilly ultimately wins in court and retatrutide is deemed a biological product, it would fall outside section 503A, meaning traditional pharmacy compounding of it would not be authorized under the FDCA in the way it is for drug products. If FDA's position is ultimately upheld, retatrutide remains regulated as a drug, leaving the legal questions about compounding to the ordinary 503A framework.

All that said, it's certainly not an authorized substance for compounding at present, so ... don't.

The Senate Health, Education, Labor & Pensions Committee took what was a spectacularly bad bill and made it vastly better. That does not mean the so-called “SAFE" Drugs Act is fixed. But it means that the voices of patients and pharmacists were heard. 

As introduced, the bill would have eviscerated shortage-drug compounding — the ability for pharmacies to help patients continue their medication therapy when an FDA-approved drug is unavailable. That language is gone.

But this amended bill provides smart protections. The amended bill adds mandatory reporting of serious adverse events by traditional compounding pharmacies through FDA’s MedWatch system. APC supported that approach and worked with committee staff on a practical, appropriate way to do it.

Responsible compounders want accountability. We want patient-safety measures that are workable, focused on actual risk, and designed to protect patients. What we cannot stand by an allow are provisions that restrict legitimate pharmacy compounding while leaving the real bad actors untouched.

To be clear: APC and its members helped put this solution on the table. However, we still have concerns. The bill’s interstate dispensing reporting provision may conflict with existing law as presently written, and we will continue working to address that as the bill heads to the Senate floor.

For now, I am grateful to Senate HELP Committee staff for hearing our perspective and creating a far better bill.

Thanks to advocacy by APC and a broad coalition, California AB 1990 has been stripped of nearly all its original provisions.

Gone are the sweeping restrictions that would have imposed drug-manufacturing requirements on pharmacies: sourcing API only from the drugmakers themselves, mandatory impurity profiling of API, batch and expiration testing of preparations at expiration, extensive supply-chain verification, and penalties of $1,000 per dose plus license revocation. Collectively, those provisions could have made lawful, patient-specific GLP-1 compounding practically impossible in California – even though permitted under federal law.

What remains is largely an advertising bill. But one especially bad provision survives.

AB 1990 would require advertising for a compounded GLP-1 to reproduce side effects, warnings and other risk information from the labeling of an FDA-approved drug containing the same active ingredient – unless the advertiser can prove particular information is irrelevant.

That may sound reasonable until you think about it.

The clinical trials and labeling for an FDA-approved drug apply to that specific product – its formulation, strength, dosing, delivery system and studied patient population. They cannot simply be generalized to a different compounded medication. Yet the bill would effectively require pharmacies to do exactly that, while placing the burden on them to decide which warnings do and do not apply.

That is not meaningful patient education. It is a functional impossibility – and an invitation to litigation regardless of which choice a pharmacy makes. AB 1990 has been dramatically improved. But leaving this provision in place is still bad lawmaking.

It may be a distinction without a difference, but my understanding of FDA’s 503A bulks list recommendation process is this:

When FDA evaluates a nominated substance, that evaluation is typically tied to the specific use or indication for which the substance was nominated. Any FDA concerns raised in that review are usually concerns about that use, not all uses.

But if FDA ultimately recommends that the substance not be included on the 503A Bulks List, that recommendation is not indication-specific. It applies to the substance itself – meaning all uses of that substance.

• Estimated nurse time of 5.90 hours for the first visit, 4.97 hours for the second, and 6.61 hours for the third
• Round-trip travel averaged 1.27 hours
• Patient assessment and documentation averaged 1 hour 3 minutes
• Across visits, patient assessment and documentation accounted for 23.08% of tasks, patient education 15.66%, and vascular access care and lab monitoring 14.65%

Mean drug administration time for home IVIG is 3 hours 58 minutes — and it ranged from 1 hour 50 minutes to 6 hours 50 minutes across patients.

The National Home Infusion Foundation published an important series of studies in #InfusionJournal on the time required by home infusion nurses to initiate care in the home for patients on IV anti-infectives, monoclonal antibodies, and Ig. The key findings of these studies illustrate that the billable home visit represents only a portion of the nursing resources required to safely deliver home infusion.  

Some key findings include:

- On average, it takes 5.43 hours of nursing time (Pre-visit work + first home visit+ travel) to admit a patient on IV anti-infectives and 5.33 hours for monoclonal antibodies. (Does not include drug administration time.)
- About 40% of nursing patient care occurs outside the patient home to perform care coordination, communication, and documentation. 
- Drug-administration time is additive to the reported workload figures.  Administration time averaged 49 minutes for anti-infectives and 1 hour 55 minutes for monoclonal antibodies.
- When pharmacist and nurse time are combined, it takes 4.24 total hours of clinical work to onboard a patient for IV anti-infectives. This work occurs before the first visit when billing begins.
- The mean drug administration time for home IVIg is 3 hours 58 min.

Bottom line: Much of the work that makes home infusion safe and effective occurs outside the patient home, and the majority of time spent by nurses and pharmacists to onboard patients is not recognized by current reimbursement structures. 

Sincere thanks to Jennifer Charron Charron, Michelle Simpson, PharmD, BCSCP, MWC Danell Haines, PhD and the National Home Infusion Association Nursing Task Force members for their work to design and implement these studies.

Pardon my rant....Posting a shortened version of my column from the current issue of INFUSION. 

Home Infusion is not Convenient - It's Essential

When we talk about home infusion, inevitably the word “convenient” works its way into the discussion. I would argue that we should remove this term from our vocabulary. “Convenient” implies a mild preference, a nice-to-have perk. Using  “convenience” to describe home infusion services, isn't just underselling it— it's fundamentally promoting a misunderstanding of it.

When a child can stay in school instead of missing days for treatment, that’s continuity of education and social development. When a working adult
can keep their job because they don’t have to spend entire weekdays in an infusion center, that’s economic stability. When an immunocompromised patient can avoid repeated exposure to health care settings filled with pathogens, that’s risk reduction with potentially life-or-death implications.

Home infusion is one of the clearest, most tangible expressions of patient-centered care and yet it’s still too often framed as an optional upgrade rather than a foundational access point.

When home infusion is treated as a “convenience,” it becomes easier to restrict coverage, to impose arbitrary limitations, to prioritize cost-containment
over patient preferences and outcomes. It subtly signals that this mode of care is expendable and that patients can just as easily go somewhere else.

Home infusion is infrastructure that creates either a life organized around illness or a life that makes room for everything else. So, please retire the word “convenience” when talking about home infusion. It’s not just inaccurate—it’s dismissive—and does not reflect the true impact of the services and what it means to patient’s lives.

Following up on the pass-through article from last week. I covered what these units are and how they work, but not much on what actually gets tested.

CAG-015 has one table covering both designs. Six tests.

On a clean air device, airflow and HEPA filter leak are required. There's a filter and a blower, so there's something to test.

On a static pass-through, neither of those applies. No filter, no fan.

Interlock, door seal, and viable surface sample are required on both.

Then there's preparation ingress and egress, and that's the one worth knowing about. Optional on a clean air device, required on a static unit. It's the only test that goes the other direction.

Which makes sense if you think about what each design is doing. The purged unit has filtered air clearing the chamber and you can test that directly. The static unit has nothing clearing it, so you test the transfer instead.

One more thing on that test. The footnote says it has to be performed if there's no manufacturer airflow data and the unit sits between a classified and an unclassified space. So if you've got an older pass-through and nobody can find the paperwork on it, optional stops being optional.

💨 Your cleanroom’s pressure reading is a floor, not a target.

In sterile compounding, it’s easy to treat your pressure differentials like a finish line. If the gauge hits the number, we log it and move on.
But sitting exactly at the regulatory minimum means your compliance is running on a razor-thin margin.

In Article 3 of The Pass-Through, we’re diving into the physics of both sides of the glass—and what your gauges stop telling you the moment a door actually opens.

One Force, Two Directions: While a positive-pressure cascade protects sterile preps from the environment, hazardous compounding flips the script. USP <800> requires a negative pressure of 0.01" to 0.03" w.c. to contain dangerous residues. Mixing up these targets on your logs is an instant audit red flag.

The Static Illusion: Whether positive or negative, those numbers only describe a sealed room. The second someone walks through a door, that pressure barrier collapses into a brief burst of airflow.

The Wake Effect: Moving faster through a doorway actually increases air turbulence and particle drag; it doesn't reduce it.

Stop the excursion guesswork. When an HVAC downtime causes a pressure loss, do you know exactly how many minutes your hazardous or non-hazardous room can absorb before it loses ISO classification?

Summer is hard on cleanrooms, and I think we tend to blame the wrong half of it.

Two things happen at once, and they compound.

The first is that your ACPH rate drifts down. HEPA filters load, resistance climbs, and the fan that delivered 450 CFM through a clean filter might only move 380 through a loaded one. Belts stretch. Ducts leak. Sometimes a tech adjusts a damper on an unrelated service call and nobody rebalances the room afterward. None of it is dramatic, and because most pharmacies measure ACPH twice a year, you usually find out well after the fact.

The second is that humidity climbs, which is the part everyone already blames.

Here's what makes the combination worth paying attention to. Our study in the Journal of the IEST (Melton et al., 2025) found a 5.993 odds ratio for out of limit EM results once RH sits at 50% or above. And separate work from Qiu et al. found that ventilation did more to reduce bacterial growth than lowering humidity did.

So the risk factor is rising while the strongest defense against it is quietly weakening, in the same months. I'd argue that isn't two problems showing up together. It's one, and your July EM results may be telling you as much about your HVAC as about the weather.

Which is why I keep saying certification data and EM data shouldn't live in two different binders.

The next article in The Pass-Through gets into how ACPH is calculated, what makes it drift between visits, and why more air is not automatically better.

Here is something that surprises most pharmacists the first time they hear it.

Your HEPA filter is rated 99.97% efficient at 0.3 microns. Most people assume that means 0.3 microns is the smallest particle it can catch.

It is actually the HARDEST one.

Particles bigger than 0.3 microns get caught by inertia. They cannot turn fast enough around the filter fibers, so they slam into them. Particles smaller than 0.3 microns move erratically from Brownian motion and bump into fibers on their own.

0.3 microns sits in the middle. Too small to carry much inertia, too big to run  into a fiber. That is why it is called the Most Penetrating Particle Size, and why HEPA filters are rated at the point where they perform WORST rather than at an easier one.

Practically, you cannot see a failing HEPA filter. A pinhole, a frame seal gap, or a crack in the media is invisible to the eye and will slowly pass contaminated air into your ISO classified spaces. That is why CETA CAG-003 requires HEPA integrity testing at every certification, with a photometer scanning the entire filter face and frame.

This week in The Pass-Through: all four capture mechanisms, what HEPA testing actually measures, and how to spot a filter heading toward failure before your certifier does.

Most people judge a chewable tablet by what happens in their mouth.

Does it taste good?

Is it easy to take?

But when we make the medication, we have to think about what happens after that.

Chewable formats can start breaking sensitive ingredients down earlier in the process. 

So making something more convenient for the patient can create a new delivery problem.

That’s where liposomal technology comes in.

The simplest way I describe it is as the Trojan horse of medicine.

The active ingredients are surrounded by a phospholipid barrier designed to help protect them as they move through the digestive system.

The chewable is the format.

The liposomal system is what allows us to ask more from it.

Sometimes the biggest obstacle between a patient and a treatment is the needle.

Some patients just aren’t comfortable administering an injection.

Some travel frequently and don’t want to carry supplies.

Others simply don’t want their life rearranged around needles.

Whether oral delivery is appropriate depends on the ingredient, dose, and clinical use.

But when another dosage form is possible, it deserves to be explored.

That’s what makes liposomal chewable tablets interesting.

And that's why we put everything we have into making sure we mastered this format before we brought it to market!

Liposomals give formulators another way to approach oral delivery while giving patients a premeasured, portable format that feels completely familiar.

Every therapy has to be evaluated individually.

The larger point is that dosage form should always be part of the treatment conversation.

The best option on paper won’t be the best option for every patient’s life.

More compounded medications are assembled in America than people probably realize.

Think about an American car company.

The car might be put together in Michigan, but that doesn't mean the steering wheel, computer chips and every other component were manufactured there.

Compounding pharmacy works in a similar way.

We're not creating sildenafil or another active pharmaceutical ingredient from scratch in the back of the pharmacy.

A lot of those ingredients are manufactured overseas, with India and China playing a big role in the supply chain.

And contrary to what may now be popular belief, this is a net positive for the end result.

Repackers break larger quantities into sizes a pharmacy can actually use and provide the documentation needed to verify the ingredient's identity and source.

Then the ingredient reaches the compounding pharmacy.

From there, we’re taking that ingredient, verifying it, formulating it and turning it into the medication the patient was prescribed.

So “assembled in America” is probably the more honest way to describe it.

The ingredients can come from all over the world.

The finished medication is still prepared here, for one specific patient, by the pharmacy responsible for getting it right.

When I was in pharmacy school rotations, there was a pharmacy in Middle Village that felt like stepping back into the 1950s.

And I mean that in the best possible way.

Everybody knew the pharmacist.

People would walk in, ask for him by name, and start telling him what was going on.

Maybe they had an injury or they weren’t feeling right or had a question about a med they were taking.

And they wanted to talk to HIM.

What was crazy to me was how natural the relationship seemed.

He wasn’t just some guy behind the counter filling a prescription.

He was somebody the neighborhood knew well enough to go to when they needed help figuring out what to do next.

I think that’s a pretty interesting version of healthcare because you can’t manufacture that kind of relationship overnight.

You get it from being there, knowing the people who walk through the door, and being useful to them over and over.

We talk a lot about making healthcare more convenient, and no doubt there’s a lot of value in that.

But there was something pretty cool about watching people walk into a pharmacy already knowing exactly who they wanted to talk to.

BPC-157 is best understood through the lens of professional sports.

When your recovery is worth $100 million, your incentive structure changes.

BPC is back in the news after an FDA advisory committee recommended allowing compounding pharmacies to make it available by prescription.

That's not the same as FDA approval, and it doesn't change the fact that the human research is still limited. 

But it does show how much interest there is in anything connected to faster recovery.

Professional sports is probably the easiest place to understand the "why".

If I'm sitting at home injured with a $100 million contract and my entire career depends on getting my body back out there, I'm going to ask about everything.

I'm going to ask what could help, how quickly it might work, what the risks are, and whether I'm allowed to take it.

BPC-157 is prohibited by WADA, so this isn't something a tested athlete can casually experiment with.

But the demand itself isn't hard to understand.

For a regular person, recovering a few weeks faster might mean getting back to the gym or playing golf again.

For a professional athlete, those same few weeks could affect a roster spot, a playoff run, the next contract, or how many years they have left to earn at that level.

That's why I don't think peptide demand can be explained as a wellness fad.

When getting healthy can affect an athlete’s career and millions of dollars, you can understand why anything tied to faster recovery gets their attention.

There's an interesting business lesson in the Shazam app. 

Did you know it was almost a total failure?

The basic idea was always great. You hear a song somewhere and want to know what it is. 

But before smartphones, the experience was awkward. 

You had to dial a number, hold the phone up to the song, and wait for the answer to come back by text.

That's a lot of steps for something that should feel instant.

Then smartphones changed the whole experience! 

The microphone was already part of the device. You opened the app, it listened and the answer came back immediately. Perfect.

Shazam didn't need people to adopt a new behavior anymore - the need to jump through hoops to get value from the product completely disappeared. 

So the lesson is simple:

Your idea could be awesome, but there is such a thing as TOO early. 

Some things you accept as "normal" could be massive friction points. 

And forces outside of your control could change the entire experience of your product overnight.

I thought my grandfather’s name was going to help me on my hospice pharmacy rotation.

Turns out, not exactly.

I was starting a rotation at a hospice pharmacy and the pharmacist in charge was going through the names of the students.

When he got to mine he stopped and asked if I was related to Rocco Stella, my grandfather.

At that point I’m thinking: This is great! He knows my grandfather! We have something to talk about.

Then he tells me: 

"Your grandfather failed me"

Not quite the warm intro I was hoping for!

I remember thinking: Oh no. This is going to be a wild 30 days!

It ended up becoming one of the rotations that had the biggest impact on my career.

He put me in the compounding lab, where I learned to make rapidly dissolving morphine tablets for hospice patients. (I still have videos on my phone from 2015 of me making them.)

I had grown up around pharmacy my entire life, so I already knew the business. Or at least I thought I did.

Getting into that lab was different.

There are things you can learn from your family, your professors, and hearing stories about an industry your whole life.

Then there are things you only understand once somebody puts the work in front of you and says, go do it.

One of the first kids' vitamin gummy company almost died on the shelf.

Marty Rifkin and his wife started a supplement company doing what everyone else was doing:

Capsules, tablets, ointments, suspensions.

Then they tried gummies. Specifically, kids' vitamin gummies.

The product idea was great. 

But the execution almost killed them.

They'd ship to supermarkets, and the gummies would bleed color through the bottle. 

Supermarkets would open the boxes to clear bottles full of muddy, off-color gummies and pull the product right off the shelves.

Most people would've quit there, or just switched to a different idea.

Marty didn't. 

He kept iterating. 

Color formulations. Stability testing. Coatings. Bottle materials. 

They went through what most people would consider a brutal R&D cycle just to keep their product on a shelf.

Eventually they cracked it. 

The company is called Lil Critters by Vitafusion. You've seen them in every supermarket in America.

A few years later they sold to Church & Dwight (the Arm & Hammer people) for $650 million.

I think about this story a lot.

The R&D piece is what people don't see, and what would typically get glossed over in a post like this. 

The reality is that every successful gummy company has a graveyard of failed batches behind it. Gummies are NOT an easy category, for a variety of reasons.

That's also why this is a REAL category and not a fad. 

The barrier to entry IS the R&D. 

Anyone can have the idea. 

Almost nobody is willing to spend two or three years in the lab figuring out why the colors bleed or the dose won't work.

When I was a kid, I found vaginal pH medication in my pharmacist grandfather’s toolbox one day.

If you know pharmacy, boric acid is a pretty strange thing to find sitting next to screwdrivers and a hammer.

So I asked him about it.

“Grandpa, what are you doing with this?”

And he got annoyed.

He looked at me like I had no idea what I was talking about. Which, to be fair, I didn’t.

He had tried all the regular stuff for ants. Sprays, detergents, whatever he could get from the hardware store. 

None of it worked the way he wanted.

So he used boric acid.

In his mind, this was obvious. He understood the chemistry. He understood what it did. He knew exactly why it worked.

I just saw a prescription item in a toolbox and was puzzled.

That’s one of the funny things about growing up around old-school pharmacists.

They had this very practical kind of knowledge. Not always polished or explained in some perfect academic way. But it came from decades of knowing what things do, how they work, and where they can be useful.

It was a great lesson in realizing the old guy in the garage understood the science a lot better than I did.

In 1920s Germany, confectioner Hans Riegel spent years making candy in his kitchen with his wife with almost no success. 

He'd stay up with his wife at the stove every night with rolling pins and crockpots, grinding sugar, trying different forms, and delivering whatever he made on a bicycle to local shops.

Then one day, he shaped his product into a bear.

It became wildly popular extremely fast, and he had found his winning product. 

He combined his name (Hans Riegel) with the town he was from (Bonn) and called the company Haribo.

100 years later, nobody walks through a grocery store thinking about the guy who invented the gummy bear. It's just part of the world now.

Hans wasn't a businessman. He wasn't a marketer. He wasn't a scientist in the traditional sense.

He was a confectionery artist.

That's the part nobody talks about when they look at the gummy industry today. 

Every successful gummy company traces back to someone who actually knew how to make candy.

This is also why no compounding pharmacy has cracked this yet.

You can be the best pharmacist in the country and still not have the first clue how to turn an active ingredient into a stable, shelf-safe, good-tasting gummy. 

That's a different craft.

So when we decided to build out gummies at Precision, we didn't try to fake our way through it.

We partnered with actual confectionery scientists. People who've spent their whole careers doing this work.

You can't shortcut this kind of thing. 

It's been a long road, but at the end of the day...our product will speak for itself.

The pharmacy manufacturing system failed once before in 1804.

And it looks like it’s failing again.

There was a time when your pharmacy was just down the corner. Zero other options. That was the entire business model.

You bought the ingredients. You made the medicine. People came in, talked to the pharmacist, got what they needed, and went home.

Very hands-on. Very local. And always close to the patient.

That world means a lot to me. 

But pharmacy has had moments where the old setup couldn’t keep up with what medicine was becoming.

Morphine was isolated and commercialized by Merck. Manufacturing changed. Drug development changed. The entire scale changed.

At some point, the corner pharmacy was not built to make every type of medication patients needed anymore.

So the industry built new infrastructure around it.

And I think we’re in one of those moments again.

It’s not exactly the same but the pressure feels that way.

GLP-1s changed demand. Telehealth changed access. AI is speeding things up. DTC pharma is changing how patients find and buy their medication.

All of that is hitting compounding pharmacy at the same time.

And there’s no way the traditional model was built for that kind of volume.

That doesn’t mean the old model goes away. It shouldn’t.

There will always be a place for hands-on, patient-specific compounding. That’s the heart of it.

But high-volume telehealth is a different thing.

You need the clinical side, but you also need infrastructure. Compliance. Technology. Capacity. Quality control. The ability to take on volume without the whole thing getting messy.

The industry isn't going away from what compounding is.

Just into a version that can keep up with how patients are getting what they need..

An FDA advisory committee recently voted 8–6–1 to recommend adding TB-500-related substances to the 503A Bulks List.

More specifically, the committee considered TB-500 free base and TB-500 acetate as two separate bulk drug substances.

That distinction matters.

FDA staff had recommended against adding either form, citing limited characterization, no identified human studies and major unanswered questions about safety and effectiveness.

But during the hearing, the FDA raised an even more basic problem:

What substance does “TB-500” actually refer to?

People often talk about it like it's one clearly defined thing.

You order TB-500. The vial says TB-500. Everyone moves on.

But FDA said TB-500 is a common name, not a standardized pharmaceutical name, and that different salts, derivatives and even different active moieties may be sold under it.

That is why FDA evaluated TB-500 free base and TB-500 acetate separately.

FDA official Russell Wesdyk put the problem bluntly:

“When you write a script for TB-500, what form do you think your patients are getting? Does anybody know? I certainly don’t, and that’s a challenge for us.”

That is a huge issue.

A pharmacy needs to know exactly which bulk ingredient it is receiving, whether the certificate of analysis describes that same substance and which specifications and testing methods apply to it.

Those safeguards don't mean much when the name on the prescription, the label and the documentation may refer to different chemical forms.

You can't really shrug and say, “Well, the website called it TB-500!”

The online conversation usually starts with whether it helps with recovery, inflammation or whatever else people are taking it for.

As a pharmacist, I have to start with a more basic question:

Which form of TB-500 is actually being discussed, and how would a pharmacy verify that the ingredient matches the documentation?

The committee recommended moving both forms forward.

That does not put them on the list today, and it is not FDA approval.

FDA still has to decide whether to accept the recommendation through the formal regulatory process.

If it does, defining exactly what each form is, and making sure prescriptions, labels and testing documents all refer to the same substance, will be essential to making that pathway work.

“Liposomal” on a product sheet is only the starting point -- it doesn’t tell you anything about formulation quality.

Two chewable tablets can use the same terminology and still be built with very different levels of precision and care.

At Precision, we focus on the details that determine real-world performance:

- Particle size control

- Compatibility between active ingredients and lipid systems

And, critically, batch-to-batch consistency at scale.

The tablet is what the patient experiences, but the real science happens long before that moment.

It’s in the formulation design, the process control, and the testing that ensures everything performs as intended every time.

As liposomal products become more widely used, healthcare companies have an opportunity to go beyond surface-level claims and partner with teams who can demonstrate how those systems are actually built.

That's why I still think rotations are so valuable.

You can go through school thinking you have a pretty good idea of what pharmacy looks like.

Then you spend a month somewhere totally different and realize how much of the profession you haven't even seen yet.

My favorite entrepreneur is my father. Hands down.

I’m not saying that because he’s my dad. I’ve watched the guy up close my whole life, and the amount of scrap and grit he has is just crazy.

He came up in a different version of pharmacy (Retail and Long Term Care Pharmacy). There are things he’s been through and figured out that I probably still don’t fully appreciate.

For a long time, the relationship was what you would expect: I was learning from him.

I’d ask him questions, watch how he handled things, and try to pick up little pieces from the way he thought through a problem or found a way around something that looked stuck.

A lot of what I know about business started there.

What’s been really cool, especially over the last few years, is that the relationship has changed a little bit.

Now we have this funny relationship where I still call him when I’m running into something, but he’ll call me too.

He could very easily be the guy who says, “I’ve been doing this longer than you’ve been alive. I’m good.”

A lot of people get older, get experienced, build some success, and then they kind of lock in. 

They stop wanting to be taught or challenged. They start treating every new thing like it’s just a worse version of the old thing.

My dad never did that.

He has the scars and the experience, but he’s still willing to listen. Still willing to ask questions. Still willing to look at something new and not immediately treat it like nonsense.

That might be the part I respect the most.

Anybody can be old school. But it’s a lot harder to be old school and still open minded.

Chewables are kind of a funny problem in pharmacy.

You make something easier for the patient to take, and in the process you can make your job of delivering the ingredient harder.

Take B12 or glutathione.

Put it in a chewable and you have a dosage form a lot of people would rather take than swallowing another pill.

But the second you start chewing it, you're also starting to break that molecule down.

So now you have to think past the chewable itself.

One way to do it is with liposomal technology. 

The simple version is you surround the ingredient with a fat barrier that helps protect it as it moves through the gut.

I like this example because it shows how much more goes into formulation than picking a format.

A gummy can taste great.

A chewable can be convenient.

A tablet can be easy to manufacture.

But none of those things by themselves tell you what happens to the ingredient once somebody takes it.

That's why I think the formulation conversation has to go further than, “What form should we put this in?”

You also have to figure out what you're asking that form to do.

I recently shared an interaction where I spent time helping a patient understand a complicated therapy decision.

Someone asked a very fair question:

How much were you able to bill for your time and expertise?

The answer was $0.

My response was that this was a whole other conversation.

So, let's have it.

I strongly support provider status and broader reimbursement for pharmacist-provided services. It would be a huge step forward for our profession and for the patients who already rely on pharmacists for so much of their care.

But it also got me thinking about what happens after we get there.

Pharmacists are already doing so much beyond dispensing. Provider status would create broader pathways to recognize and reimburse that clinical value.

We need that.

But I spent years behind a retail pharmacy counter, and I can't think about this without thinking about the pharmacist who will actually be standing there providing these services.

Prescriptions waiting. Phones ringing. Patients at the counter. Vaccines to give. Counseling questions. Insurance problems. Someone calling out. A technician needing help. Somehow you're supposed to be in five places at once.

A lot of pharmacists are still living that every day.

So yes, I want provider status.

But I also want to know what happens when we add more reimbursable clinical services to that environment.

Does that revenue support pharmacist overlap or additional technician hours?

Is there actually time built into the day to provide the service?

Do metrics and expectations change when responsibilities change?

And yes, I think it's fair to ask whether compensation eventually reflects the additional professional value pharmacists are generating.

Metrics and goals aren't the problem. Pharmacy is still a business. But those goals have to be attainable with the people, hours, and resources available.

Because if we're asking a pharmacist to spend meaningful time with a patient as a provider, that time has to come from somewhere.

It can't just become one more box to check between everything else.

There are logistics to figure out too. Credentialing, documentation, billing, denials, whose NPI is used and how reimbursement actually flows.

None of these questions make me less supportive of provider status. They make me want us to get the implementation right.

Pharmacists have spent years taking on more clinical responsibility, expanding access to care, and proving what we're capable of doing.

I want provider status to move that forward.

I just don't want the pharmacist behind the counter to hear, "Great news, we're providers now," followed by another responsibility added to an already impossible Tuesday.

If we're going to recognize pharmacists as providers, let's also give them the environment to actually practice like providers.

Organ transplantation has always come with a tradeoff. Save the organ, but pay for it with a lifetime of immunosuppression. That tradeoff may finally be starting to shift.

Start with the medications we already use. Tacrolimus and other calcineurin inhibitors remain the backbone of most transplant regimens. What is changing is how precisely we use them. Better monitoring and more individualized dosing are helping us balance rejection risk against the long-term toxicity of immunosuppression. Sometimes innovation isn't a new drug. It's using the drugs we already have better.

The pipeline is where things get interesting.

Newer approaches are targeting specific parts of the immune response rather than broadly suppressing it. We're also seeing progress in antibody-mediated rejection. These therapies target CD38, potentially addressing the plasma cells and other immune cells involved in donor-specific antibody production and graft injury rather than relying only on broad immunosuppression or antibody removal.

For highly sensitized patients, the change may be even more consequential. New desensitization approaches such as imlifidase can rapidly reduce IgG antibodies that would otherwise make a donor incompatible. For patients who have historically faced years of waiting because nearly every available organ triggers a positive crossmatch, that could open a path that wasn’t available previously.

Then there’s immune tolerance.
Regulatory T-cell therapies take a fundamentally different approach. Rather than simply suppressing the immune system, the goal is to retrain the immune response toward tolerance.

This summer, the FDA approved the first regulatory T-cell-based immunotherapy. It isn't approved for solid-organ transplantation, but its use in allogeneic stem-cell transplant marks an important milestone for an approach researchers have been pursuing for years.

None of this means tacrolimus is disappearing or that transplant recipients are about to stop taking immunosuppressants.

But the direction is changing.

We are getting better at using the medications we have, targeting specific mechanisms of rejection, overcoming antibody barriers that once prevented transplantation, and exploring whether the immune system can eventually be taught to tolerate a transplanted organ.

For a field built around balancing rejection against the consequences of preventing it, that's an exciting shift.

A pharmacy can have a perfect policy manual and still fail operationally.

But if the team doesn’t understand it, trust it, or know how to apply it in the flow of daily operations, it is only a document.

Successful pharmacy operations require more than written procedures. They require:

Training - ensuring teams understand not only what to do, but why it matters.

Communication - creating clarity around expectations, changes, and the reasons behind the process.

Ownership - building a culture where compliance is part of everyone’s role, not just the responsibility of a compliance department or pharmacy leader.

Practical systems - designing workflows that fit the reality of patient care, staffing, technology, and competing priorities.

The strongest compliance programs are not the ones with the biggest manuals. They are the ones where the right process becomes the easiest process to follow.

Compliance should support pharmacy teams, not create another obstacle for them to overcome.

Because compliance should work in practice, not just on paper.

That stayed with me.

I was just a girl who loved science and wanted to help people.
